title: Guidelines for Selecting or Modifying Logos
authors: Henderson, P. W.; Cote, J. A.
key_findings: (As summarised by Kim & Lim 2019) Logo design characteristics (active, balance, cohesive, complex, depth, organic, parallel, proportion, repetition, representative, round, symmetric) were related to correct recognition, false recognition, affect and familiar meaning.
Three underlying design dimensions: elaborateness (complexity, activeness, depth), naturalness (representative, organic) and harmony (symmetry + balance).

Guidelines by objective: high-recognition logos = very natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate; low-investment logos = less natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate; high-image logos = moderately natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate.
Figurative logos depicting familiar objects need less learning and are recognised more easily than abstract ones.
practical_applications: Brief a new mark as 'harmonious + moderately elaborate'; choose figurative/natural when there is little media budget to teach an abstract mark.
limitations: Full text not read this session; findings come from Kim & Lim (2019) review footnotes.

US student sample, black-and-white logos, late-1990s stimuli; later cross-national work (Henderson et al. 2003; van der Lans et al. 2009) reportedly supports the three dimensions but colour/motion were not tested.

title: Does Your Company Have the Right Logo? How and Why Circular- and Angular-Logo Shapes Influence Brand Attribute Judgments
authors: Jiang, Y.; Gorn, G. J.; Galli, M.; Chattopadhyay, A.
key_findings: Five experiments: circular logos activate 'softness', angular logos 'hardness' associations, shifting attribute judgments (shoe rated more comfortable with a circular logo, more durable with an angular one; sofa softness; company customer-sensitivity).
Mechanism is mental imagery in visuospatial working memory: effect disappears under visual (not verbal) load and for people low in imagery disposition.
Shape works even as an incidental prime, not only as the logo.

No main effect on overall attitude; attitude/WTP rose only when the headline stressed the same attribute the shape implies (congruence). A headline stressing a different attribute removed/disrupted the shape effect.
practical_applications: Match shape language (round vs angular) to the attribute the brand claims (comfort/care vs durability/precision) and keep the headline on the same attribute.
limitations: Simple lab logos, fictitious brands, student/mTurk samples (N 69-306 per study); small effect sizes (partial eta-squared ~.04-.09).
Authors note real logos are complex and shape meaning depends on context (a cross means different things for a church vs a hospital).

title: A comprehensive review on logo literature: research topics, findings, and future directions
authors: Kim, M. J.; Lim, J. H.
key_findings: Reviews 124 logo studies (30 years) in six topics: theory, design/redesign, typeface/shape/colour, additional elements, outcomes, practical applications.

Redesign: new logos lose processing fluency; committed consumers judge redesigns more negatively (Walsh et al. 2010, 2011); remedies = figurative marks, repeated multi-channel exposure, launch communication.
Evolutionary (small) vs revolutionary (large) redesign; revolutionary used when strategy changes or to shed a negative image (Airey 2009, practitioner).

Shape: angular/heavy = more masculine, rounded/slender = more feminine (Lieven et al. 2015); logo frames feel protective under high risk (Fajardo et al. 2016); asymmetry linked to excitement (Bajaj & Bond 2018; Luffarelli et al. 2019).
Colour: Labrecque & Milne (2013) report a negative relation between colour differentiation from a dominant market leader and brand equity in some categories.
M&A/co-brand logo options: keep both, fuse, use the stronger one, or create new; little evidence on which is best.
practical_applications: Use as the map of logo evidence; check each claim against its primary study before treating it as fact.
limitations: Narrative (not meta-analytic) review; repeats popular colour statistics (e.g. '62-90% of judgments based on colour', 'colour raises recognition 80%') from non-peer-reviewed sources without critique.
license: copyrighted (copy found on a university course site)

title: Building a unique brand identity: measuring the relative ownership potential of brand identity element types
authors: Ward, E.; Yang, S.; Romaniuk, J.; Beal, V.
key_findings: 1,281 in-market identity elements, 13 packaged-goods categories, 19 countries; 'Competitive Intensity' (HHI-based) measure of uniqueness potential.
Characters, logos and logotypes have the highest potential for unique ownership; colour is hardest because competitors share it heavily.
Competitive intensity varies within an element type, so execution matters.
practical_applications: Invest first in a character/mascot or a distinctive logo/logotype; treat colour as a supporting cue, not the only one.
limitations: Abstract only; FMCG categories; static, de-branded elements shown one at a time.

title: Exploring the uniqueness of distinctive brand assets within the UK automotive industry
key_findings: Replicates Ward et al. (2020) in a high-involvement category: 44 de-branded assets of top-12 UK car brands, 206 respondents.
Logo is the most uniquely ownable asset; fonts, slogans and colours show low uniqueness concentration.
No gender or generational differences in uniqueness.
Reports an industry-wide lack of consistent use of non-logo assets and frames it as an opportunity for brands willing to use colour/font/slogan consistently.
practical_applications: Do not assume a font or colour is 'ours' — test whether people name the brand from it; protect the logo first.
limitations: Convenience/snowball sample (mean age ~29), one country and category; assets shown statically and individually; no sound or character assets tested.

title: Building Distinctive Brand Assets
key_findings: (Per search summaries of the book and its contents) A distinctive asset must be unique (evokes only this brand) and famous (most category buyers link it to the brand); chapters cover fame and uniqueness metrics and the fame x uniqueness grid.
Grid advice (secondary): invest in unique-but-not-yet-famous elements; avoid famous-but-not-unique elements that competitors share.
practical_applications: Run a simple fame/uniqueness test on each candidate asset before writing it into a brand book.
limitations: Book not read; publisher page blocked; content known only from secondary summaries. Practitioner-oriented book from the Ehrenberg-Bass school.

title: Evidence concerning the importance of perceived brand differentiation
authors: Romaniuk, J.; Sharp, B.; Ehrenberg, A.
key_findings: Existence confirmed; widely cited as Ehrenberg-Bass evidence that few buyers perceive their brand as different or unique, supporting 'distinctiveness over differentiation'.
practical_applications: Cite only as the origin of the distinctiveness-vs-differentiation debate.
limitations: Not read; year listed inconsistently (2004/2007/2010) across catalogues. Critics argue explicit self-report underestimates perceived differentiation.

title: Answering critics
key_findings: Rebuts critiques: growth comes mainly from penetration but loyalty also rises slightly (double jeopardy); cites longitudinal work (2003, 2012, 2014 JBR) against 'cross-sectional only'.
Argues attitude-predicts-behaviour findings reflect regression to the mean; behaviour shapes attitudes more than the reverse.
Several replies are dismissive rather than evidential (e.g. 'pseudo-science', asking critics to publish data).
practical_applications: Shows the school's own position; pair with critics for a balanced view.
limitations: Self-defence by the institute, undated, informal tone.

title: In the battle between salience and differentiation, bothism wins
key_findings: Argues Ehrenberg-Bass overstates by dismissing differentiation, and Thomaz overstates by saying distinctiveness does not work.
Reports Thomaz citing a Google/YouTube study of thousands of ads in which distinctiveness was not among the top-10 performance drivers.
Advice: keep a list of distinctive assets for salience AND a clear position for relative differentiation.
practical_applications: Brand book should hold both: distinctive assets (how we are recognised) and positioning (why choose us).
limitations: Opinion column; studies mentioned were not checked.

title: 'Byron Sharp is ignoring 60 years of published work'
key_findings: (Search summary) Argues How Brands Grow rests on Ehrenberg's stable-market assumptions, that growth depends on perceived differentiation, and that mental/physical availability lack clear measurement.
practical_applications: Reminder that distinctiveness alone is not a growth strategy.
limitations: Page did not load; only search-snippet content; polemical.

title: Recognisably You
key_findings: Database of 12,000+ assets from 900+ brands; only ~15% reach 'gold' (instant, unique link to the brand when shown alone).
Brands with many strong assets reported 31% more likely to be considered and 38% more likely to be used than brands with few.
Advice: test recognition without the logo; combine visual, verbal and sonic cues; set fixed vs flexible guardrails; track performance.
practical_applications: 'Cover the logo' test for every template; separate fixed elements from flexible ones in the brand book.
limitations: Vendor content, proprietary method, correlational (big brands have more famous assets — reverse causality likely), no sample details.

title: Do logo redesigns help or hurt your brand? The role of brand commitment
authors: Walsh, M. F.; Winterich, K. P.; Mittal, V.
key_findings: The greater the change in roundedness of a previously angular logo, the more negatively strongly committed consumers evaluate it; weakly committed consumers respond neutral-to-positive.
Negative logo evaluation spills over into lower brand attitude among committed consumers.
practical_applications: Before a rebrand, involve or pre-brief the most loyal customers; prefer evolutionary change for brands with a loyal base.
limitations: Abstract and press coverage only; 632 US undergraduates, two shoe brands, lab redesigns.

title: 'Starbucks effect': Committed customers don't like logo redesigns
key_findings: Describes Walsh/Winterich/Mittal design: Adidas and New Balance logos, slight vs considerable redesign by a professional designer, 632 students, attitude measured before and after.
Researchers recommend asking committed customers for input, notifying them before reveal, making them feel like insiders.
practical_applications: Rebrand communication plan: loyal-customer preview first.
limitations: University press release; no effect sizes.

title: Corporate rebranding failure and brand meanings in the digital environment
key_findings: Qualitative case of Gap's 2010 logo change (launched 6 Oct, old logo back 12 Oct 2010): 1,000+ Facebook posts plus Twitter and designer forums in under a week.
Brand meanings polarised (hostile and supportive) among managers, consumers, designers and marketers, shaping the failure; brand meaning is co-created online, so firms must expect public critique.
practical_applications: Treat a rebrand as a public conversation: explain the why, stage the change, monitor reactions daily in launch week.
limitations: Abstract + Lund University news summary only; single case.

title: Is a Company Known by the Company it Keeps? Assessing the Spillover Effects of Brand Alliances on Consumer Brand Attitudes
authors: Simonin, B. L.; Ruth, J. A.
key_findings: Main study (n=350) and two replications (n=150, n=210): attitudes toward a brand alliance spill over to later impressions of each partner brand.
Brand familiarity moderates these effects; partners do not necessarily gain or lose equally.
practical_applications: Co-branding/partner logos transfer meaning both ways; the less familiar partner is more affected — choose partners whose image you want to share.
limitations: Abstract only; product alliances (not retailer-carries-brand logos); 1990s US samples.

title: Co-branding logo guidelines (Red Hat-led)
key_findings: Lead brand's template, fonts, colours and voice govern; partner logo goes second; partner colours and style stay out.
Lockups: horizontal (wide partner logos), stacked (tall), vertical (square/narrow); clear space minimum = height of the 'R'; logos matched in visual size and weight.
Three or more brands: tri-brand, co-brand + partner, or equal-weight logo wall.
Always get permission to use a partner logo, even if used before; misuse includes unequal weights, custom templates, mixing illustration styles, AI-generated co-brand logos.
practical_applications: Template for 'our logo + supplier/partner logo' rules in any brand book.
limitations: One corporation's internal rules; not evidence of effectiveness.

title: Branded lockups
key_findings: Co-branded lockup: logos visually equal, vertically centred, partner logo not taller than the core symbol, thin grey divider equal to logo height, clear space = x-height of 'a'.
Defers to the partner's own co-branding standards when they exist.
Partner lockups max 1-2 per asset, placed in a corner related to the core logo, max twice core-logo height.
practical_applications: Concrete numbers to copy into a partner-logo section.
limitations: Single company practice.

title: Voice and Tone — Mailchimp Content Style Guide
key_findings: Voice = constant personality; tone = adapts to situation and the reader's emotional state.
Four voice traits (plainspoken, genuine, translators, dry humour) written with 'X but not Y' pairs (e.g. smart but not snobbish; weird but not inappropriate).
Clarity over entertainment; consider reader's state (relieved, confused); when unsure, keep a straight face; mascot is not given its own voice.
practical_applications: Use the voice-trait + 'but not' pattern and a tone-by-situation table in any brand voice guide.
limitations: Company practice, no outcome data.

title: Microsoft's brand voice: above all, simple and human
key_findings: Separates message (what) from voice (how); voice constant, tone adapts from serious to empathetic to light by context and customer state of mind.
Three principles: warm and relaxed; crisp and clear; ready to lend a hand.
Style tips: key takeaway first, talk like a person, short everyday words, cut every excess word, write for scanning.
practical_applications: Three-adjective voice principle with behavioural style tips is a compact model for small brands.
limitations: Company practice, English-language.

title: How to create brand guidelines (Shopify blog)
key_findings: Typical sections: logos (variants, sizing, clear space, colour), typography, colour palette (names, hex, hierarchy, combinations), imagery (photo, illustration, icons), audience, voice and tone, grammar/style.

Small-business advice: define personality/point of view before colours; start with logo + palette + type; write how-to-use rules with do's/don'ts and examples; a preliminary guide can be a few pages, full ones 15-80 pages.
practical_applications: Basis for the section order of BRAND_GUIDE_TEMPLATE.md.
limitations: Vendor blog; craft advice.

title: Designing Brand Identity: An Essential Guide for the Whole Branding Team
key_findings: (Per table-of-contents listings) Standard practitioner textbook; includes 'Standards + guidelines', 'Standards content', brand books and online brand tools within a 'Managing assets' phase. Multiple editions (3rd-5th).
practical_applications: Reference for full brand-book scope when a client needs more than the template.
limitations: Book not read; TOC only via search summaries.

title: Conceptualizing, Measuring, and Managing Customer-Based Brand Equity
key_findings: Customer-based brand equity = differential effect of brand knowledge on consumer response to the brand's marketing; brand knowledge = awareness + image (associations).
Awareness = recognition (confirm prior exposure when shown the brand) + recall (retrieve the brand from a category/need cue); recognition matters more when decisions are made at the point of sale.

Associations should be favourable, strong and unique; information congruent with existing associations is learned more easily, though unexpected inconsistent information can sometimes create stronger associations; incohesive images reduce what is recalled.
Measurement: indirect (recall/recognition, free association, ratings of associations) and direct (compare response to branded vs unbranded/fictitious version) approaches are complementary.
practical_applications: Small-business brand check: unaided recall question + aided recognition + 'three words you link with us' free association.
limitations: Conceptual paper (no new data); the Ehrenberg-Bass school challenges the attitude-to-behaviour direction.

title: Binet presents fast, cheap, predictive Share of Search metric
key_findings: Share of Search = a brand's organic searches / all brands' searches in the category, free from Google Trends.
Correlated with market share in cars, energy and mobile handsets and led it (up to ~12 months for cars); the gap 'Extra Share of Search' predicts share movement.
Caveats: not a silver bullet; conversion depends on price etc.; not all searches are positive.
practical_applications: Monthly Google Trends comparison of the brand name vs 2-4 local competitors as a free brand-health line.
limitations: Industry presentation, not peer-reviewed; small local brands may have too little search volume for Trends to register.

title: Investigating the effects of consistent visual identity on social media
key_findings: 2x2 between-subjects experiment (consistent vs inconsistent corporate visual identity x organisation type) on social media.
Consistent visual identity significantly improved appreciation of the identity, attitude toward the company, perceived reputation and intention to commit to the company on social media.
practical_applications: Evidence for keeping templates, palette and logo use stable across a social feed.
limitations: Abstract only; sample and stimulus details not seen; single experiment, Indian context.

title: (title not retrieved — Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights article on communication consistency and hotel brand equity)
key_findings: (Search summary) Survey of 223 five-star hotel guests: communication consistency positively related to all brand-equity dimensions, most strongly brand trust, image and perceived quality.
practical_applications: Supports one voice + one visual system across all touchpoints.
limitations: Only search snippet; title wording not confirmed; cross-sectional survey, one sector.

title: Exciting red and competent blue: the importance of color in marketing
authors: Labrecque, L. I.; Milne, G. R.
key_findings: (Per Kim & Lim 2019) Hue, saturation and value relate to brand personality dimensions (e.g. saturation positively, value negatively, with ruggedness), and colour can shape purchase intention via personality.
practical_applications: Choose palette by intended personality, then test — not by colour-meaning charts.
limitations: Not read; JAMS 40(5):711-728; colour meanings vary across cultures.
